title: Lady Be Good
one_line: After overshooting its Libyan base, the crew parachuted into the desert; all nine died.
status_why: The wreck, remains, and diaries explain the loss; precise navigation failures and one crew member's whereabouts remain unresolved.

aircraft.operator: United States Army Air Forces; 514th Bombardment Squadron, 376th Bombardment Group, Ninth Air Force
aircraft.engine_type: Pratt & Whitney R-1830-43 Twin Wasp, air-cooled radial piston engines
aircraft.livery_notes: Desert pink over earlier olive drab is described in later wreck-photo analysis; white tactical number 64 is documented. April paint standard and underside shade were not verified. Name lettering on the port nose is disputed. Dimensions are type-manual values converted using 0.3048 m/ft and 0.0254 m/in.

to.name: Soluch, intended return after the Naples harbor mission

planned_waypoints.name: Naples harbor, Italy: bombing objective; exact aimpoint not recovered

site.description: Original wreck resting area on a gravel plain at the Calanscio/Calanshio sand-sea region in southeastern Libya. Historical astro-fix, not modern GPS precision. Nearby bailout and the northward walking trail are distinct locations. Remaining wreckage was removed in 1994.

terrain_box.why: Visualization bounds chosen by the researcher: roughly 53 km east–west and 72 km north–south, centered on wreck, bailout area and southern markers. This is not an historical search perimeter. The walking trail extends much farther north and needs a separate globe view.

environment.notes: Sand and dust were reported at the field. No aircraft-specific wind observation, visibility measurement, temperature or cloud-height record was recovered. The 1150 GMT group departure is not an individual weather-observation timestamp.

Group mission summary item K says clear with ground haze. No measured visibility or layer heights are stated there. This describes the attacking group, not a timed observation from the missing bomber. Ground haze is not entered as a cloud layer.

environment.place: Return flight toward Libya, night of 4–5 April
environment.notes: Museum history account reports flight above cloud cover at night. Cloud genus, coverage, base and top are unknown; narrative tailwind explanations are not wind measurements.

environment.place: Bailout and original crash area, early 5 April by crew dating
environment.notes: Nighttime desert descent. No site weather log or supported moon illumination calculation was obtained. The 11-knot northeast wind in the later simulator is an assumed input and is not used as historical weather.
Diary reports a warm sun, breeze from northwest and a very cold night. 315 degrees only converts the named compass sector; it is not a measured azimuth. Position and UTC observation time are unknown.
Diary reports a very warm afternoon and no breeze. No breeze is qualitative; no measured wind speed or temperature is supplied.

environment.place: Crew walking route in dunes, 8 April
environment.notes: Diary reports wind and continuous blowing sand. Wind direction, speed, visibility and dune position at that time are unknown.

environment.place: Five-person final camp, nights around 9 April
environment.notes: Diary estimates nights around 35 degrees, interpreted as Fahrenheit in the American crew context. Conversion: (35−32)×5/9 = 1.6667 C. This is a rough personal estimate, not a thermometer record. North wind is qualitative; camp coordinate is from later recovery, not an observation fix.

track.engine_note: Departure from Soluch on 4 April. Individual takeoff clock is disputed; no instrument values recovered.
track.method: The group departure time in s1 is not assigned to the individual bomber.
track.locator: Toner 4 April; Ripslinger first Sunday; association aircraft history

track.engine_note: Outbound flight separated from formation. No verified position, speed or altitude is available for aircraft 64 here.
track.method: Narrative stage only; no interpolated route.

track.engine_note: Return turn near the Italian part of the mission.
track.method: Martinez reports a navigator-log departure course of 140 degrees at 20:52, time zone and true/magnetic reference unspecified. Original sheet not obtained. A planned course is not assigned as a measured aircraft heading.

track.engine_note: Bombs released or jettisoned; release position and aircraft state are unknown.
track.method: Diary transcription says 22:00; clock zone unspecified. Not the group bombing time in s1.

track.engine_note: Return toward Libya. A 150-degree course appears in the quoted Graves Registration reconstruction.
track.method: A reported reconstructed course, not a measured heading sample; true/magnetic reference not established. hdg_deg remains null because the source gives a course, not an instrument heading.
track.locator: World War II section, quoted investigation conclusion

track.engine_note: Radio request for help near Benghazi/Benina. The reported 330-degree reading is a bearing, not an aircraft heading.
track.method: Accounts describe multiple calls; original ground radio logs and exact UTC sequence not obtained.
track.locator: Lost; quoted investigation conclusion; Failure to Acknowledge

track.engine_note: Probable passage near Soluch followed by continued flight inland.
track.method: Aircraft identity and exact overhead position were not instrument-recorded. No base coordinate is used as an airborne fix.

track.engine_note: Crew abandons the bomber with fuel depleted. Eight survive their descents; the bombardier does not join them.
track.method: Diaries give 02:00 landing versus 02:10 bailout, with no verified clock zone. Ground recovery positions are not substituted for airborne exit positions.
track.locator: Toner 4 April; Ripslinger first Sunday; engine-control discussion

track.engine_note: Uncrewed belly impact. Engines 1–3 feathered; number 4 controls in operating position. Fuselage broke behind wing.
track.method: Published historical astro-fix converted from 26°42′45.7″ N, 24°01′27″ E. Approximate original wreck position, not a modern survey. Instrument states at discovery do not give impact speed or attitude.

events.title: Group departs Soluch
events.detail: 4 April 1943: the group summary gives 1150 GMT as departure time. This is a group reference, not a verified individual takeoff time for Lady Be Good.
events.caption: The bomber group departed Soluch. Lady Be Good's exact takeoff time isn't known.

events.title: Lady Be Good takes off
events.detail: 4 April: the engineer’s diary transcription gives takeoff as 15:10. Another military summary gives 14:50 and later accounts differ; the individual UTC time is unresolved.
events.caption: Lady Be Good took off on April 4. The exact time isn't known.

events.title: Formation separates
events.detail: 4 April: sand and poor visibility disrupted the formation. Lady Be Good returned separately from the other bombers.
events.caption: Sand and poor visibility disrupted the formation. Lady Be Good returned separately from the other bombers.

events.title: Group attacks Naples harbor
events.detail: 4 April: the group report records bombing between 1735 and 1745 GMT at 23,500–25,000 feet. These values describe the attacking group and do not establish Lady Be Good’s position or altitude.
events.caption: The group bombed Naples harbor. Lady Be Good's position and altitude during the attack are unknown.

events.title: Return turn is logged
events.detail: 4 April, 20:52 on an unspecified clock: Martinez reports a 140-degree departure-course entry in the navigator’s log. This is a later transcription; the original sheet was not obtained.
events.caption: The navigator noted a return course. The exact time isn't known.

events.title: Engineer records bomb release
events.detail: 4 April, 22:00 on an unspecified clock: the engineer records releasing bombs. The entry alone does not establish bombing Naples rather than jettisoning over water.
events.caption: The crew released the bombs, but where they fell is unknown.

events.title: Crew requests radio help
events.detail: Late 4 April or early 5 April: accounts describe a request for a bearing and a malfunctioning direction finder. The quoted Army reconstruction gives a 330-degree bearing from Benina; the original radio log was not recovered for this research.
events.caption: The crew requested radio directions after their direction finder malfunctioned.

events.title: Aircraft is heard near base
events.detail: Around midnight on the witnesses’ clocks, personnel heard a bomber near Soluch and fired flares. Retrospective testimony identifies it as probably Lady Be Good; no exact overhead fix follows from the sound.
events.locator: Failure to Acknowledge, McCain letter and Liberandos passage
events.caption: Personnel near Soluch heard a bomber and fired flares. It was probably Lady Be Good.

events.title: Benghazi call may go unanswered
events.detail: Around midnight: Martinez says a separate Benghazi radio station failed to answer the pilot because an enemy aircraft was suspected. This contested account rests on later interviews, not a cockpit recording.
events.locator: Failure to Acknowledge; The Lady That Didn’t Come Home
events.caption: The pilot's call may have gone unanswered because a radio station suspected an enemy aircraft.

events.title: Fuel becomes depleted
events.detail: Early 5 April by crew dating: the copilot records running out of fuel. Later examination found three propellers feathered and the fourth engine configured to operate.
events.caption: The bomber ran out of fuel. Three propellers were later found set to reduce drag.

events.title: Crew bails out
events.detail: Early 5 April: the copilot records landing in the desert at 02:00; the engineer gives bailout at 02:10. These are unconverted crew clock readings, not verified UTC times.
events.caption: The crew parachuted into the desert early on April 5. The exact time isn't known.

events.title: Uncrewed bomber strikes desert
events.detail: After abandonment, the bomber struck a gravel plain and skidded roughly 700 yards. Its fourth engine detached and its fuselage broke behind the wings; the exact impact time, speed and attitude are unknown.
events.caption: The empty bomber struck the desert and skidded about 700 yards. An engine detached and the body broke.

events.title: Group reports missing aircraft
events.detail: The 5 April confirmation says its telegraphic summary was filed at 0200 GMT. Aircraft 64 with its pilot was unaccounted for; a second bomber was also still unaccounted for in this initial report.
events.caption: Lady Be Good and another bomber were still missing when the group sent its initial summary.

events.title: Eight men begin walking
events.detail: 5 April: eight men assembled without the bombardier and walked northwest. The copilot recorded a few rations and half a canteen of water, rationed by capful.
events.caption: Eight crew members gathered without the bombardier and walked northwest, sharing food and half a canteen of water.

events.title: Walking and resting alternate
events.detail: 6 April: the diary records resting at 11:30 until 17:00, then walking and resting through the night in a 15-minute walking, 5-minute resting pattern. The clock zone is unknown.
events.caption: The crew rested during the day, then walked through the night with frequent short breaks.

events.title: Crew reaches sand dunes
events.detail: 8 April: the copilot records reaching dunes amid blowing sand. The men were weakening and their eyes were affected.
events.caption: The crew reached dunes in blowing sand. They were weakening, and their eyes were affected.

events.title: Three continue for help
events.detail: The copilot places the separation on 9 April; the engineer mentions it under Saturday 10 April. The engineer and two gunners continued while five men remained behind.
events.caption: The engineer and two gunners continued to seek help. Five crew members stayed behind.

events.title: Engineer makes final entry
events.detail: 11 April: the engineer’s final entry says they were still struggling through dunes to find water. It does not give a location or establish when he died.
events.caption: The engineer's last diary entry describes struggling through dunes for water. His exact time of death is unknown.

events.title: Copilot makes final entry
events.detail: 12 April: the copilot’s last written entry reports no help and another cold night. Blank later diary spaces do not establish anyone’s exact time of death.
events.caption: The copilot's last diary entry describes another cold night without help. Exact times of death are unknown.

events.title: British patrol buries unidentified remains
events.detail: February 1953: a later account says a British convoy photographed and buried unidentified remains while crossing the sand sea. Their proposed connection with the missing gunner was raised decades later and remains unproved.
events.caption: A British convoy reportedly buried unidentified remains in 1953. A connection to the missing gunner remains unproved.

events.title: Early aerial sighting is reported
events.detail: 16 May 1958: Martinez reports a sighting by oil-survey personnel, followed by another on 15 June. Other accounts instead emphasize November 1958; discovery chronology remains conflicted.
events.caption: Oil surveyors reportedly spotted the wreck in May and June 1958. The first sighting's date is uncertain.

events.title: November sighting enters later accounts
events.detail: 9 November 1958 is the aerial-discovery date repeated in the 2021 physics article. This is retained alongside the May and June accounts rather than called the unique first sighting.
events.caption: An aerial sighting was also reported in November 1958. Whether it was the first remains uncertain.

events.title: Oil surveyors reach the wreck
events.detail: 27–28 February 1959: Bowerman, Sheridan and Martin reached and examined the bomber in the detailed later accounts. Institutional summaries often place the ground visit in March.
events.locator: Coordinate provenance; ground expedition narrative; Crash Site Discovery
events.caption: Oil surveyors reached and examined the wreck in early 1959. The exact date is uncertain.

events.title: Military search begins
events.detail: May 1959: Army mortuary and Air Force personnel investigated the empty wreck and began searching for the crew. Fuller and Neep were key Army investigators.
events.caption: Army and Air Force personnel investigated the empty wreck and began searching for the crew.

events.title: Boots reveal the northward trail
events.detail: 16 June 1959 according to Lowery: searchers found flight boots about 19 miles north of the wreck. Further searches followed old vehicle tracks and found discarded equipment and parachute arrows.
events.caption: Searchers found flight boots north of the wreck, then discarded equipment and arrows made from parachutes.

events.title: Another arrow marker is found
events.detail: 20 July 1959: an additional parachute-and-stone arrow was found during a return trip toward the wreck. Its mapped position is a later approximation.
events.locator: Lowery p.73; southern Parachute Marker, Items placemark
events.caption: Another arrow made from parachute material and stones was found. Its exact location is uncertain.

events.title: First search closes without remains
events.detail: 2 September 1959 in Lowery’s account: the search team was airlifted out after extensive effort. The working explanation was that the men’s remains had been covered by sand.
events.caption: The first search ended without finding remains. Searchers thought sand had covered them.

events.title: First investigation report is dated
events.detail: 17 November 1959: the Quartermaster bibliography identifies a report by Fuller and Neep on the lost bomber and the 1959 search. The full report was not obtained.
events.caption: An investigation report covered the lost bomber and the 1959 search.

events.title: Five crew members are found
events.detail: 11 February 1960: oil workers found five crew members together, with equipment and the copilot’s diary. The 2024 documentary describes the discovery message arriving on 12 February.
events.locator: Five Crewmembers Found; documentary transcript, discovery-message passage
events.caption: Oil workers found five crew members' remains together, along with equipment and the copilot's diary.

events.title: Operation Climax expands the search
events.detail: Spring 1960: a joint Army–Air Force operation used ground parties, aircraft and helicopters to seek the four still missing. It followed the February recovery.
events.locator: Operation Climax section and film captions
events.caption: Army and Air Force teams searched by ground and air for the four crew members still missing.

events.title: A gunner is found farther north
events.detail: 12 May 1960: oil workers found Shelley. Relative-distance accounts conflict, so his published recovery coordinate is kept separately from claims about miles walked.
events.locator: Operation Climax; Lowery p.74; Coordinates Used
events.caption: Oil workers found a gunner's remains farther north in May 1960.

events.title: Flight engineer is found
events.detail: 17 May 1960: a helicopter search found Ripslinger. His diary was recovered; the published coordinate lies south of Shelley’s, contrary to some institutional retellings.
events.locator: Operation Climax; Lowery p.74; Coordinates Used
events.caption: A helicopter search found the flight engineer's remains and recovered his diary.

events.title: Final organized search ends
events.detail: Late May 1960: Operation Climax ended with two men still missing. The later bombardier discovery was separate.
events.caption: The organized search ended in late May 1960. Two crew members were still missing.

events.title: Second investigation report is dated
events.detail: 20 June 1960: the Quartermaster bibliography identifies the final-search report by Fuller and Neep. Its text and appendices were not located in an accessible digital copy.
events.caption: A second investigation report covered the final organized search.

events.title: Bombardier is found near bailout area
events.detail: 11 August 1960 in the detailed later accounts: the bombardier was found near the original descent area with a partially deployed parachute. Nearby abandoned flying equipment and spent flares identified the survivors’ assembly area.
events.locator: Woravka paragraph; Woravka placemark; August discovery
events.caption: The bombardier's remains lay near the descent area with a partially opened parachute. Equipment marked the survivors' gathering.

events.title: Crew memorial window is dedicated
events.detail: January 1961: a memorial stained-glass window was unveiled at Wheelus. It was later moved to the U.S. Air Force museum.
events.caption: A memorial window honoring the crew was unveiled at Wheelus, then moved to the U.S. Air Force museum.

events.title: Components support materials research
events.detail: April 1968: an RAF desert team recovered components for materials study. The wreck’s long exposure provided evidence about deterioration during storage.
events.locator: Epilogue; Walker materials-study account; materials testing
events.caption: A Royal Air Force team recovered components to study how long desert exposure affected the materials.

events.title: Wreckage is moved for safekeeping
events.detail: August 1994: Libyan authorities removed the remaining wreckage to Tobruk. The original crash-site coordinates therefore do not locate the surviving airframe today.
events.locator: Epilogue; The Lady That Didn’t Come Home
events.caption: Libyan authorities moved the remaining wreckage to Tobruk for safekeeping in 1994.

events.title: Moore photograph is assessed
events.detail: 2001–2002: Martinez investigated a photograph from the 1953 convoy and sought an osteologist’s opinion. The photograph could not establish identity and did not close the missing gunner’s case.
events.caption: A photograph of the unidentified remains could not establish their identity. The missing gunner's case remained unresolved.

perspectives.label: Reciprocal bearing and overflight
perspectives.held_by: Graves Registration reconstruction as quoted by Quartermaster history; Joseph Portney; later institutional histories
perspectives.claim: The bomber passed its base and continued inland while its crew believed it was still returning over the Mediterranean. The quoted official reconstruction proposes a reciprocal-bearing error, followed by fuel depletion and bailout; it does not supply a continuous measured route.

evidence_for.text: The quoted investigation gives a 150-degree course and a 330-degree Benina reading.
The wreck, missing parachutes, diary and northward trail establish inland abandonment and the subsequent survival attempt.
Portney’s abstract identifies missing return dead-reckoning entries as a contributor.

evidence_against.text: No continuous flight record or complete radio log was obtained; the exact recognition and interpretation failures cannot be reconstructed.
A failed or unanswered radio exchange could have compounded the error. These explanations need not be mutually exclusive.

ending.description: Same inland wreck and bailout as the physical-evidence account; precise flight course remains uncertain.

perspectives.label: Unanswered Benghazi radio call
perspectives.held_by: Mario Martinez, drawing on retrospective interviews and letters
perspectives.claim: Martinez gives greater causal weight to an unanswered request at Benghazi radio headquarters, distinct from Benina and Soluch. He argues that suspicion of a German aircraft prevented useful help from reaching the crew.

evidence_for.text: His own account identifies a 1985 interview with an officer and a separate Benghazi station.
The National Archives narrative also describes an unsuccessful request for help.

evidence_against.text: The original tower log and interview recording were not obtained here; decades-later recollection does not settle each call’s timing or receipt.
This does not refute the physical evidence of inland flight or establish the bomber’s exact position.

ending.description: Same wreck and survival sequence; responsibility for the failed recovery of position differs.

perspectives.label: Simulated final right turn
perspectives.claim: A later simulator explores a trimmed, one-engine descent with a right turn. Its numerical output is a visualization hypothesis, not historical telemetry.

evidence_for.text: Attempts to match bailout vicinity, wreck position and impact geometry.

evidence_against.text: Fuel, trim, wind and aircraft state were assumed; Holder instead describes a leftward arc expected by consulted pilots.

ending.description: Published simulation reaches near the wreck after a turn; exact simulated endpoint is not tabulated here.

track_override.method: Ed Truthan, Flight Simulator study; assumed starting state, not an observed exit fix. No absolute UTC available.
Ed Truthan model output; reported elapsed descent 7 minutes 36 seconds and mean descent about 300 ft/min. Mean is not assigned as an instantaneous vertical speed.

perspectives.label: Possible enemy damage
perspectives.held_by: William G. Holder; discussed cautiously by Mario Martinez
perspectives.claim: A recovered engine reportedly contained damage or a fragment associated with a 20-mm projectile. Holder suggested possible enemy fire near the target; this does not establish when the damage occurred or that it caused the loss.

evidence_for.text: Both authors discuss the recovered-engine finding.

evidence_against.text: No dated laboratory report, matching sortie attack report or broader battle-damage pattern was obtained.
The crew diary instead identifies becoming lost and running out of fuel.

ending.description: No supported alternative endpoint or flight path; possible contributing damage only.

perspectives.label: Unidentified burial may be Moore
perspectives.held_by: Mario Martinez and the former British convoy participant who contacted him
perspectives.claim: Unidentified remains photographed and buried in 1953 might have been the still-missing gunner. The proposed location is an approximate regional inference, not a recovered grave or accepted identification.

evidence_for.text: A participant supplied a photograph and convoy account; the proposed region could fit the northward walk.

evidence_against.text: The osteologist could not determine identity from the photograph. No identifying objects, re-exhumation or DNA result establishes Moore.

ending.description: The flight is unchanged. Only the possible later whereabouts of one crew member differ.

perspectives.label: Salvaged parts carried a curse
perspectives.held_by: Later folklore repeated by Holder and documentaries
perspectives.claim: Stories linked subsequent aircraft troubles to reused parts from the bomber. They are folklore, not a supported cause of this accident or of the later accidents.

evidence_for.text: Reuse and subsequent mishap stories were published.

evidence_against.text: Temporal association does not establish causation; no supporting technical finding is presented.
Ordinary navigation failure, fuel depletion and the desert ordeal have direct physical and diary evidence.

ending.description: No evidence-based alternative flight or endpoint.

evidence_points.label: Soluch landing-ground vicinity
evidence_points.detail: Secondary historical coordinate: 31°40′20″ N, 20°14′35″ E. Approximate field vicinity, not a runway threshold or recorded takeoff fix.

evidence_points.label: Original wreck astro-fix
evidence_points.detail: Historical survey position, approximately located; wreck later removed.

evidence_points.label: Later mapped wreck footprint
evidence_points.detail: Truthan’s revised map position; approximate satellite-image interpretation.

evidence_points.label: Bombardier recovery area
evidence_points.detail: Minute-resolution coordinate; parachute failure inferred from recovery evidence.

evidence_points.label: Survivors assembly area
evidence_points.detail: Modelled from relative distance southwest of bombardier; not surveyed.

evidence_points.label: Flight boots
evidence_points.detail: Approximate mapped trail position; first search clue.

evidence_points.label: Southern parachute arrow
evidence_points.detail: Arrow and shroud lines; approximate mapped position.

evidence_points.label: Arrow with named harness
evidence_points.detail: Harness associated with Moore; approximate mapped position.

evidence_points.label: Northern parachute arrow
evidence_points.detail: Stone outline on rocky knoll; approximate mapped position.

evidence_points.label: Five-person final camp
evidence_points.detail: Published minute-resolution recovery coordinate; exact walking distance disputed.

evidence_points.label: Gunner Shelley recovery area
evidence_points.detail: Published minute-resolution recovery coordinate; north of engineer.

evidence_points.label: Hypothesized unidentified-burial region
evidence_points.detail: Martinez regional hypothesis only; not an identified grave.

witnesses.who: Returning bomber pilot and personnel at Soluch
witnesses.said: Paraphrase: a bomber was heard passing nearby after the returning section landed, and flares were fired. Its identity as Lady Be Good was inferred.
Paraphrase: a bomber wreck was seen during aerial surveys; a ground party later examined the empty aircraft. The dates of first sighting differ between accounts.

witnesses.who: Former British signals mechanic on a 1953 convoy
witnesses.said: Paraphrase via Martinez: companions photographed and buried unidentified remains before his delayed vehicle arrived. He later supplied the photograph; he did not identify the remains at the time.

why_it_matters: The wreck supplied long-exposed aircraft components for materials and storage research [s9, s24]. The case is used to teach direction-finding ambiguity, cross-checking and survival limitations [s17, s18]; no specific regulatory change caused by it was verified.

conflicts.a: Engineer transcription: 15:10. AFHRA telegraphic group summary: 1150 GMT.
conflicts.b: AFHRA statistical group summary: 14:50, zone not visible; 2021 paper: 14:15. Group and individual times may also describe different things. No local-to-UTC conversion is asserted.

conflicts.a: Telegraphic summary lists 25 B-24Ds; copilot diary says 28 planes.
conflicts.b: Statistical sheet lists 27 initiated sorties and 17 completed; Holder gives 26. Definitions and changing mission status may differ; no harmonized count is invented.

conflicts.about: Abort short of target or reach Naples vicinity
conflicts.a: Quartermaster summary and NARA say the bomber turned back before the target.
conflicts.b: Engineer records bombs released at 22:00; Martinez interprets a late return turn near Naples. A release entry is not proof of hitting the target.

conflicts.about: Radio bearing, equipment failure and responsibility
conflicts.a: Quoted Army conclusion proposes reciprocal-bearing error involving 150/330 degrees.
conflicts.b: NARA emphasizes malfunction and missing help; Martinez emphasizes an unanswered Benghazi call. Ground HF/DF readings and onboard radio-compass readings are sometimes conflated in later accounts.
Engineer transcription gives bailout at 02:10. These may be approximate readings of different actions; neither has a verified UTC basis.

conflicts.about: Date of separation into two parties
conflicts.b: Engineer: separation mentioned under Saturday 10 April. The precise departure of the three is not resolved.

conflicts.a: Martinez specifies 16 May and 15 June 1958; Quartermaster history and Smithsonian give May.
conflicts.b: NARA emphasizes November 1958; the 2021 paper gives 9 November. These may include multiple sightings rather than a single discovery.

conflicts.a: Detailed expedition accounts and coordinate provenance give 27–28 February 1959.
conflicts.b: NARA and Quartermaster summaries put a ground visit in March. Do not collapse these into a fabricated exact arrival timestamp.
2011 KMZ revised footprint: 26.714241 N, 24.022475 E. Historical survey and later imagery interpretation differ; site precision is approximate.

conflicts.a: Quartermaster and NARA give about 85 miles; association and Lowery give 78 miles.
conflicts.b: Truthan calculates about 74 miles along a simplified mapped route. Distances from bailout, wreck, inferred trail and actual dune walking are not interchangeable.

conflicts.a: Quartermaster history and NARA place Shelley 21 miles beyond the five, then Ripslinger another 26 miles north.
conflicts.b: Published recovery coordinates instead put Ripslinger south of Shelley. Lowery gives Ripslinger about 26 miles beyond the five and Shelley 11.5 farther; Truthan reports about 27.46 and 9.96. The institutional distance paragraph is unsuitable for plotting.

conflicts.a: Lowery reports 115.5 miles from bailout for Shelley.
conflicts.b: Smithsonian gives 111 miles; other accounts use different start points or simplified trails. No exact total walked distance is known.

conflicts.a: Holder describes a leftward sweeping arc expected by experienced pilots.
conflicts.b: Truthan models a right turn for assumed trim and wind. Neither is recorded telemetry; trim at abandonment is unknown.

conflicts.a: Holder says the investigation found no water jugs and records a thermos partly full of coffee.
conflicts.b: Later accounts describe water and food aboard; Davis says early visitors found canteens in raft compartments. Items removed before inspection and container terminology could matter. No inventory quantity is accepted.

conflicts.a: Wartime searches initially treated the missing bomber as likely lost at sea.
conflicts.b: The recovered inland wreck and diaries disprove that endpoint. It is a rejected historical assumption, not an equally supported current theory.

unknowns: Exact UTC accident date/time. Crew dating places bailout in the early hours of 5 April, but their clock zone was not established. Depending on that zone the UTC date could be 4 or 5 April. date_utc is therefore null; the mission began on 4 April UTC.

Time convention: only explicitly labelled GMT in the primary group report is normalized to UTC (same historical civil time reference for this use). Unlabelled local clocks, diary times and day-only discoveries are not converted or padded with midnight timestamps. Null event times retain the date in detail and narrative order.

No flight recorder, cockpit voice recorder, radar, ADS-B, ACARS or satellite-log time series was found or expected for this 1943 bomber. The nine main track stages are not a sampled trajectory and must not be interpolated as measured flight.

Full 17 November 1959 and 20 June 1960 Quartermaster reports, appendices, original field notebooks and survey maps were not retrieved. Their existence, dates and authors were checked in the opened bibliography; conclusions used here are explicitly mediated through later accounts.
The brief attribution to Graham Barlow could not be substantiated. The opened Quartermaster bibliography names Myron C. Fuller Jr. and Wesley A. Neep for both reports.

No Hatton survival diary was located. The journals found and checked belong to copilot Toner and engineer Ripslinger. Woravka’s reported notebook is a separate item; no complete primary scan was obtained.
Original navigator W6 sheet, all outbound positions and original ground radio logs were not obtained. The 20:52/140-degree entry is Martinez’s report of the sheet, not a newly read instrument record.

Exact Italian turning point, bomb-release location, approach to the Libyan coast and inland flight course. A city or airfield center must not be used as proof the aircraft crossed that exact coordinate.
Exact number, wording, order, timestamps, frequencies and receipt of Benina, Soluch and Benghazi radio calls. No verbatim radio quotation is supplied from retrospective recollection.

Whether direction-finder malfunction, a reciprocal interpretation, ground non-response or several failures best explain continuing inland. A 330-degree bearing is not itself an aircraft heading or a two-dimensional fix.
True versus magnetic reference for reported 140/150/330-degree values. No numerical declination correction has been applied.

Individual aircraft altitude, airspeed, groundspeed, attitude, vertical speed, angle of attack and fuel quantities throughout the mission and descent. Group 23,500–25,000-foot bombing altitudes are not assigned to this aircraft.
Actual trim, engine shutdown times, autopilot state, bailout sequence and instantaneous aircraft position for each jump. Final engine-control settings cannot establish when an engine stopped.
Exact impact point versus final resting point, crash elevation and vertical terrain profile. The approximately 700-yard skid is reported, not a mapped polyline with endpoints.

A modern surveyed wreck coordinate. The old astro-fix and later satellite-footprint interpretation differ. Wreckage was removed in 1994; its exact storage position and condition in November 2026 were not verified.
Exact Soluch takeoff-strip center, threshold and elevation. The route uses a historical landing-ground vicinity from a secondary airfield study, not modern Benina coordinates or its airport codes.
Precise Naples aimpoint, full authorized flight plan, turnpoints and diversion instructions; no geographic waypoint positions were invented.

Measured cloud base/top/coverage, winds aloft, pressure, visibility, precipitation, turbulence, lightning and temperature along the flight. Absence of a report is not zero wind, clear sky or no precipitation.
Lunar phase, elevation and illumination at bailout were not verified; no full-moon or moonless-night claim is made. Later simulator wind inputs and climatology are not observations for 5 April 1943.

Exact walking line, daily positions and construction times for trail arrows. All seven plotted arrow positions come from Truthan’s model, not surveyed military fixes. Do not attach aircraft altitude or speed to this ground trail.

Exact total walking distances, local dune detours, whether later recoveries shifted from the death positions, and precise times when individuals died. Diaries establish minimum survival, not a common death time.
Moore’s remains and grave location. The approximate 28 N, 23 E proposal is not a confirmed discovery or identification; no accepted recovery was found in the 2024–2026 search.
Cause, date and operational importance of the reported projectile fragment. Full laboratory documentation and a matching combat encounter were not located.

Exact quantity of drinkable water and usable supplies left aboard at abandonment, and whether the crew could have found the wreck, used its radio or reached an oasis. Such survival outcomes are counterfactual, not established findings.

Airframe fuselage diameter, numerical wing sweep definition, exact April 1943 underside color and paint standard were not verified. They remain null or explicitly qualified rather than estimated from generic model dimensions.

No specific post-accident safety regulation demonstrably caused by this loss was found. Materials research and its use as a navigation/survival teaching case are documented; claimed rule changes without a primary record are omitted.

2024–2026 update search: the opened December 2024 PBS documentary and July 2026 retrospective supplied no verified new recovery, DNA identification or official finding. This is a bounded search result, not a guarantee that no unpublished development exists.

Access limits: current USAF Museum pages and the Air University journal PDF returned 403; the Army museum host failed to resolve. Relevant archival images, AFHRA scans, a complete archived Air University article and archived Quartermaster pages were opened instead. Failed URLs are not counted as opened sources.
memorial_note: Nine USAAF crew members left Soluch on this mission; this reconstruction remembers their lives and their families’ long wait for answers.
